lessons.title: Estimating Start-up Costs
lessons.body: Start-up costs are the one-time expenses you pay before your business opens its doors. In Africa, these often include registration fees, equipment, initial stock, and deposits. For example, a small poultry farm in Ghana might need: 500 day-old chicks at 5 cedis each (2,500 cedis), 20 bags of feed at 150 cedis (3,000 cedis), feeders and drinkers (800 cedis), a simple wooden coop (2,000 cedis), and business registration (300 cedis). That totals 8,600 cedis. You also need working capital for the first three months of rent, utilities, and labour. If your monthly rent is 400 cedis, utilities 200 cedis, and one helper at 500 cedis, that's 1,100 cedis per month, so 3,300 cedis for three months. Your total start-up cost is 11,900 cedis. To estimate accurately, use a notebook or a free spreadsheet like Google Sheets. List every item, no matter how small. Ask other business owners in your area for typical prices. Include a 10% contingency for price changes or forgotten items. For a mobile money kiosk in Kenya, you might need a licence (5,000 KES), a smartphone (15,000 KES), a float of 50,000 KES, a small table (2,000 KES), and a umbrella (1,000 KES). That's 73,000 KES. Add 10% (7,300) for safety. Your total is 80,300 KES. Remember, start-up costs are not the same as operating costs. Operating costs come later. Be realistic: if you underestimate, you may run out of money before you make your first sale. Write down every cost, then add them up. This number tells you how much you need to save, borrow, or raise from family and friends.

lessons.title: Projecting Revenue and Expenses
lessons.body: Projecting revenue and expenses means guessing how much money will come in and go out each month. Start with revenue. If you sell 20 loaves of bread per day at 10 rand each, that's 200 rand per day. In a 30-day month, that's 6,000 rand. But not every day is the same. Saturdays may be busier, Sundays slower. Use a conservative estimate: maybe 15 loaves per day on average. That gives 4,500 rand per month. Now expenses. Fixed expenses stay the same: rent 1,500 rand, electricity 300 rand, phone 100 rand. Variable expenses change with sales: flour, yeast, and packaging cost about 4 rand per loaf. For 450 loaves (15 per day x 30 days), that's 1,800 rand. Total expenses: 1,500 + 300 + 100 + 1,800 = 3,700 rand. Your projected profit is 4,500 - 3,700 = 800 rand per month. But you must also pay yourself. If you need 2,000 rand to live, you need more sales or lower costs. To project for a year, multiply monthly figures by 12, but adjust for seasonality. In many African countries, December has higher sales, while January may be slow. Use a simple spreadsheet: one column for months, rows for revenue and each expense. Sum them at the bottom. Be honest: if you are too optimistic, you will run out of cash. If too pessimistic, you may not try. Test your numbers with a friend or mentor. For a phone repair shop in Nigeria, revenue might be 5,000 naira per repair, 10 repairs per week = 50,000 naira per week, or 200,000 naira per month. Expenses: rent 20,000, parts 80,000, transport 10,000, data 5,000 = 115,000. Profit 85,000 naira. That's a start.

lessons.title: Creating a Cash Flow Statement
lessons.body: A cash flow statement tracks when money actually enters and leaves your business. It is not the same as profit. You can be profitable but still run out of cash if customers pay late. For example, a catering business in South Africa wins a 20,000 rand order in March, but the client pays in May. In March, you spend 8,000 rand on ingredients and labour. Your profit for March looks like 12,000 rand, but your cash flow is negative 8,000 rand. You need cash to pay suppliers. To create a cash flow statement, list all cash inflows (sales, loans, grants) and outflows (rent, wages, supplies, loan repayments) for each month. Start with opening cash balance. Add inflows. Subtract outflows. The result is closing cash balance, which becomes next month's opening balance. Use a spreadsheet with columns for Jan, Feb, Mar, etc. For a small shop in Tanzania, January: opening cash 500,000 TZS. Sales: 1,200,000. Loan: 0. Total inflows: 1,200,000. Outflows: rent 200,000, stock 600,000, wages 300,000, utilities 50,000. Total outflows: 1,150,000. Closing cash: 500,000 + 1,200,000 - 1,150,000 = 550,000 TZS. If closing cash is negative, you need a plan: delay payments, get a short-term loan, or increase sales. Always keep a minimum cash buffer, say 10% of monthly expenses. Review your cash flow weekly. Many African businesses fail not because they are unprofitable, but because they run out of cash. A cash flow statement helps you see problems before they happen. Update it every month with actual numbers to improve your projections.

lessons.title: Building a Profit and Loss Statement
lessons.body: A profit and loss statement (P&L) shows whether your business made money over a period, usually a month or a year. It lists revenue, then subtracts expenses to get profit. Start with sales revenue. For a fashion designer in Kenya, monthly sales might be 80,000 KES. Next, cost of goods sold (COGS): fabric, thread, buttons, and direct labour. If each dress costs 1,500 KES to make and you sell 20 dresses, COGS = 30,000 KES. Gross profit = 80,000 - 30,000 = 50,000 KES. Then operating expenses: rent 10,000, electricity 2,000, marketing 5,000, transport 3,000, phone 1,000, and your salary 15,000. Total operating expenses = 36,000 KES. Net profit before tax = 50,000 - 36,000 = 14,000 KES. If tax is 30%, tax = 4,200, net profit after tax = 9,800 KES. That is your bottom line. To build a P&L, use a simple spreadsheet. List revenue at top. Subtract COGS to get gross profit. List all operating expenses. Subtract them to get net profit. Do this for each month and for the year. Compare with your projections. If actual profit is lower, find out why: maybe sales are down or costs are up. Adjust your plan. A P&L is different from cash flow because it includes non-cash items like depreciation. For example, if you bought a sewing machine for 30,000 KES, you might depreciate it over 3 years, so 10,000 KES per year (833 KES per month) appears as an expense on the P&L but not on the cash flow. The P&L tells you if you are making a profit. The cash flow tells you if you have money to pay bills. You need both.

lessons.title: Balance Sheet Basics
lessons.body: A balance sheet shows what your business owns (assets), what it owes (liabilities), and what is left for the owner (equity) at a specific date. The basic equation is: Assets = Liabilities + Equity. For a small retail shop in Uganda, assets might include cash 500,000 UGX, inventory 1,200,000 UGX, a refrigerator 800,000 UGX, and a delivery bike 1,500,000 UGX. Total assets = 4,000,000 UGX. Liabilities: a bank loan 1,000,000 UGX and unpaid supplier bills 300,000 UGX. Total liabilities = 1,300,000 UGX. Equity = assets - liabilities = 4,000,000 - 1,300,000 = 2,700,000 UGX. Equity includes your initial investment plus retained profits. If you started with 2,000,000 UGX and have retained profits of 700,000 UGX, that matches. To create a balance sheet, list assets in order of liquidity: cash first, then inventory, then equipment. List liabilities: short-term (due within a year) like supplier bills, then long-term like loans. Equity is the difference. A balance sheet is a snapshot, not a movie. It shows your financial position on one day, like 31 December. It helps you see if you have too much debt or too much cash sitting idle. For example, if your inventory is very high, you may have cash tied up in unsold goods. If your liabilities are greater than your assets, you are insolvent. Review your balance sheet quarterly. Use a spreadsheet with two columns: left for assets, right for liabilities and equity. They must balance. If they don't, you made a mistake. This statement is required by banks when you apply for a loan. It shows you are serious and organised.

lessons.title: Break-Even Analysis
lessons.body: Break-even analysis tells you how many units you must sell to cover all your costs. At break-even, profit is zero. To calculate, you need fixed costs, variable cost per unit, and selling price per unit. For a juice bar in Rwanda, fixed costs per month: rent 80,000 RWF, salaries 120,000 RWF, utilities 20,000 RWF, total 220,000 RWF. Variable cost per glass of juice: fruit 200 RWF, sugar 50 RWF, cup 50 RWF, total 300 RWF. Selling price per glass: 800 RWF. Contribution margin per glass = 800 - 300 = 500 RWF. Break-even point in units = fixed costs / contribution margin = 220,000 / 500 = 440 glasses per month. That means you must sell 440 glasses to break even. If you sell 500 glasses, profit = (500 x 500) - 220,000 = 250,000 - 220,000 = 30,000 RWF. If you sell 400 glasses, loss = (400 x 500) - 220,000 = 200,000 - 220,000 = -20,000 RWF. You can also calculate break-even in sales revenue: fixed costs / (contribution margin / selling price) = 220,000 / (500/800) = 220,000 / 0.625 = 352,000 RWF. So you need 352,000 RWF in sales to break even. Use this to set sales targets. If your break-even is 440 glasses but you only sell 300, you need to either reduce fixed costs (e.g., move to cheaper rent) or increase price or reduce variable costs. Break-even analysis helps you understand risk. The lower your break-even, the safer your business. For a new business, aim to break even within 6 to 12 months. Track your actual sales against break-even each month. If you are consistently below, change your strategy.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Financial Projections and Analysis

Financial projections are not a formality for banks and donors. They are the management cockpit of an African agribusiness. Whether you are aggregating maize from smallholders in Tanzania, running a poultry operation in Ghana, or processing shea butter in Burkina Faso, your projections tell you how much money you need, when you need it, and whether the business can survive a bad season. This lesson gives you a practical reference for building and reading the six core financial tools in a business plan: start-up costs, revenue and expense projections, cash flow, profit and loss, balance sheet, and break-even analysis.

In African agribusiness, three realities shape every projection. First, seasonality: income arrives in harvest windows while costs run all year. Second, working capital intensity: you buy inputs or stock before you sell, so cash flow gaps are normal. Third, informality and price volatility: records may be thin, and exchange rates, fuel, and commodity prices can shift quickly. Good projections are built on realistic assumptions, documented in writing, and stress-tested against a bad year.

1. Estimating Start-up Costs

Start-up costs are everything you must spend before the business earns its first naira, shilling, cedi, or rand. Separate them into capital expenditure (one-off, long-life items) and pre-operating expenses (one-off but consumed). For agribusiness, common items include land preparation, irrigation, cold chain, processing equipment, vehicles, packaging, licences, and initial working capital for inputs or stock. Include a contingency of 10â15% because African supply chains often deliver surprises: import delays, currency movements, or transport cost spikes.

Table 1: Illustrative start-up cost estimate â small maize aggregation and milling unit (USD)
Cost itemTypeAmount (USD)
Milling equipment and installationCapital18,000
Storage and drying facilityCapital12,000
Delivery vehicle (used)Capital9,000
Business registration, licences, permitsPre-operating1,200
Initial grain stock (working capital)Working capital15,000
Packaging and brandingPre-operating2,500
Training and staff recruitmentPre-operating1,800
Contingency (10%)Reserve5,950
Total start-up requirement65,450

Source: Structure adapted from IFC/World Bank Doing Business / B-READY start-up cost methodology and FAO agribusiness investment guidance. Figures are illustrative for teaching purposes.

2. Projecting Revenue and Expenses

Revenue projections should be built from volume Ã price, not from a single sales figure. For agribusiness, volumes depend on yield, capacity, or supply available; prices depend on season, quality grade, and market channel. Show your assumptions in a table. On the expense side, split fixed costs (rent, salaries, insurance, loan interest) from variable costs (seed, feed, packaging, transport, commission). This split is what makes break-even analysis possible later.

Table 2: Illustrative three-year revenue and expense projection â maize aggregation and milling (USD)
Line itemYear 1Year 2Year 3
Volume sold (tonnes)300450600
Average price per tonne320325330
Revenue96,000146,250198,000
Variable costs (purchase, milling, transport)72,000106,000141,000
Fixed costs (salaries, rent, interest)14,50015,20016,000
Depreciation3,9003,9003,900
Total costs90,400125,100160,900
Operating profit5,60021,15037,100

Source: Presentation format adapted from IFAD Rural Finance and Agribusiness training materials and FAO Agribusiness Public-Private Partnerships toolkits. Figures are illustrative.

3. Creating a Cash Flow Statement

The cash flow statement answers one question: will there be money in the bank when I need it? It records actual cash in and cash out by month or quarter. In African agribusiness this is often the most important statement because profitability does not guarantee liquidity. A business can be profitable on paper and still fail if it cannot pay workers during the lean season. Build the statement in three sections: operating activities, investing activities (equipment, vehicles), and financing activities (loans, grants, owner equity). Always start with an opening cash balance and end with a closing balance.

â  SAFETY WARNING â CASH FLOW IS NOT PROFIT

Do not use your profit and loss statement to decide whether you can pay suppliers, staff, or loan instalments. A profitable agribusiness can run out of cash during the off-season. Never commit to loan repayments, input purchases, or expansion based on projected profit alone. Build and monitor a monthly cash flow statement, and keep a contingency reserve of at least one to three months of fixed costs. In markets with high inflation or currency volatility, review cash flow weekly, not annually.

4. Building a Profit and Loss Statement

The profit and loss (P&L) statement shows performance over a period â usually a month, quarter, or year. It follows a simple structure: revenue minus cost of goods sold equals gross profit; gross profit minus operating expenses equals operating profit; then subtract interest and tax to get net profit. In agribusiness, be careful to match costs to the correct period. If you buy stock in January and sell it in April, the purchase belongs in cost of goods sold when the sale occurs, not when the cash left the account. This is the accrual principle, and it is what makes the P&L different from cash flow.

5. Balance Sheet Basics

The balance sheet is a snapshot at a single date. It shows what the business owns (assets), what it owes (liabilities), and what belongs to the owners (equity). The fundamental identity is:

Assets = Liabilities + Equity

For agribusiness, key assets include cash, stock (grain, feed, livestock), receivables from buyers, and equipment. Key liabilities include supplier credit, bank loans, and unpaid wages. Equity includes owner capital, retained earnings, and grants treated as capital. A healthy balance sheet shows enough current assets (cash + stock + receivables) to cover current liabilities. If stock is slow-moving or receivables are overdue, the balance sheet may look strong while the business is actually fragile.

6. Break-Even Analysis

Break-even analysis tells you the minimum volume or revenue needed to cover all costs. The formula is:

Break-even volume = Fixed costs Ã· (Price per unit â Variable cost per unit)

Using the Year 1 figures in Table 2: fixed costs are 14,500 + 3,900 depreciation = 18,400. Price per tonne is 320 and variable cost per tonne is 72,000 Ã· 300 = 240. Contribution per tonne is 80. Break-even volume = 18,400 Ã· 80 = 230 tonnes. So the business must sell at least 230 tonnes in Year 1 to avoid a loss. This is a powerful negotiating and planning number: it tells you how much supply you must secure and how much market you must line up before the season starts.

Quick Reference Checklist

  • Assumptions written down: Every projection has a documented assumption for volume, price, yield, and cost inflation.
  • Start-up costs split: Capital expenditure, pre-operating costs, and working capital are separated and a contingency is included.
  • Revenue built from volume Ã price: Not a single guessed sales figure, and seasonality is shown by month or quarter.
  • Fixed and variable costs separated: This enables break-even analysis and margin tracking.
  • Monthly cash flow prepared: Opening balance, cash in, cash out, and closing balance are shown for at least 12 months.
  • P&L uses accrual matching: Costs are matched to the period when the related sale occurs, not just when cash moves.
  • Balance sheet balances: Assets equal liabilities plus equity, and current assets cover current liabilities.
  • Break-even calculated and stress-tested: You know the minimum volume and have tested a 20â30% price or yield drop.

Further Reading

  • FAO â Smallholder Business Models for Agribusiness Development
  • IFAD â Rural Finance and Agribusiness Resources
  • IFC â Agribusiness Investment and Advisory
  • ILO â Small Business Financial Management Training Materials
  • African Development Bank â Agriculture and Agribusiness

quiz.q: What is a start-up cost?
options: A) A monthly expense like rent
B) A one-time expense before opening
C) A loan from a bank
quiz.explanation: Start-up costs are one-time expenses incurred before the business begins operations.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a start-up cost for a poultry farm?
quiz.explanation: Day-old chicks are purchased once to start the flock, unlike recurring monthly costs.

quiz.q: Why should you add a 10% contingency to start-up costs?
options: B) To cover unexpected price changes
D) To pay yourself a salary
quiz.explanation: A contingency buffer covers forgotten items or price increases.

quiz.q: What is the difference between start-up costs and operating costs?
options: A) Start-up costs are monthly, operating costs are one-time
B) Start-up costs are one-time, operating costs are ongoing
D) Start-up costs are only for equipment
quiz.explanation: Start-up costs occur before opening; operating costs recur during business operations.

quiz.q: In the lesson, what tool is suggested for estimating start-up costs?
options: A) A notebook or Google Sheets
quiz.explanation: The lesson recommends using a notebook or free spreadsheet like Google Sheets.

quiz.q: What is revenue?
options: B) Money coming in from sales
quiz.explanation: Revenue is the income generated from selling goods or services.

quiz.q: If you sell 20 loaves at 10 rand each, what is your daily revenue?
quiz.explanation: 20 loaves x 10 rand = 200 rand per day.

quiz.q: Which of these is a fixed expense?
quiz.explanation: Rent stays the same each month regardless of sales.

quiz.q: Why should you be conservative when projecting revenue?
options: A) To avoid running out of cash
quiz.explanation: Overestimating revenue can lead to cash shortages if actual sales are lower.

quiz.q: What is a variable expense?
options: A) An expense that changes with sales
B) An expense that is always the same
quiz.explanation: Variable expenses fluctuate based on production or sales volume.

quiz.q: What does a cash flow statement track?
options: B) When cash enters and leaves
quiz.explanation: Cash flow tracks the timing of actual cash inflows and outflows.

quiz.q: Why can a profitable business run out of cash?
options: B) Because expenses are too low
C) Because profit is not cash
quiz.explanation: Profit is an accounting figure; cash flow depends on when payments are received and made.

quiz.q: In a cash flow statement, what is the closing cash balance?
quiz.explanation: Closing cash is calculated by adding inflows and subtracting outflows from opening cash.

quiz.q: What should you do if your projected closing cash is negative?
options: B) Get a loan or delay payments
quiz.explanation: Negative cash flow requires action like short-term borrowing or delaying outflows.

quiz.q: How often should you review your cash flow?
quiz.explanation: Weekly review helps catch cash problems early.

quiz.q: What does a profit and loss statement show?
quiz.explanation: A P&L shows revenue, expenses, and profit for a specific period.

quiz.q: What is cost of goods sold (COGS)?
options: B) Direct costs of making a product
quiz.explanation: COGS includes materials and direct labour used to produce goods sold.

quiz.q: If revenue is 80,000 KES and COGS is 30,000 KES, what is gross profit?
quiz.explanation: Gross profit = revenue - COGS = 80,000 - 30,000 = 50,000 KES.

quiz.q: What is net profit?
quiz.explanation: Net profit is what remains after subtracting all operating expenses from gross profit.

quiz.q: Why is depreciation on a P&L but not on a cash flow statement?
options: A) It is a non-cash expense
B) It is a cash outflow
quiz.explanation: Depreciation spreads the cost of an asset over time without actual cash leaving the business.

quiz.q: What is the basic accounting equation for a balance sheet?
quiz.explanation: The balance sheet must balance: what you own equals what you owe plus owner's equity.

quiz.q: Which of the following is an asset?
quiz.explanation: Inventory is something the business owns and has value.

quiz.q: If assets are 4,000,000 UGX and liabilities are 1,300,000 UGX, what is equity?
quiz.explanation: Equity = Assets - Liabilities = 4,000,000 - 1,300,000 = 2,700,000 UGX.

quiz.q: What does a balance sheet show?
options: C) Financial position at a point in time
quiz.explanation: A balance sheet is a snapshot of assets, liabilities, and equity on a specific date.

quiz.q: Why is a balance sheet useful for a loan application?
options: A) It shows you are organised
C) It shows your cash flow
quiz.explanation: Banks want to see your financial position and that you keep proper records.

quiz.q: What is break-even analysis?
options: B) Finding sales needed to cover costs
quiz.explanation: Break-even tells you the sales volume where total revenue equals total costs.

quiz.q: If fixed costs are 220,000 RWF and contribution margin per unit is 500 RWF, what is break-even in units?
quiz.explanation: Break-even units = fixed costs / contribution margin = 220,000 / 500 = 440.

quiz.q: What is contribution margin?
options: A) Selling price - variable cost per unit
quiz.explanation: Contribution margin is the amount each unit contributes to covering fixed costs and profit.

quiz.q: If break-even is 440 glasses but you sell 400, what happens?
quiz.explanation: Selling below break-even means total costs exceed revenue, resulting in a loss.

quiz.q: How can you lower your break-even point?
options: B) Reduce variable costs or increase price
quiz.explanation: Lowering variable costs or raising price increases contribution margin, reducing break-even units.
